food.text: Milan is home to the oldest restaurant in Italy and the second oldest in Europe, the Antica trattoria Bagutto. It has existed since at least 1284.
The oldest Italian book on cuisine is the 13th century Liber de coquina, or Cookbook, written in Naples. Its dishes are similar to ones eaten in Italy today.

The Liber de coquina includes "Roman-style" cabbage and a dish of small leaves prepared in the "Campanian manner". It also has a bean dish from the Marca di Trevisio, showing how the recipes drew on different parts of Italy.
Medieval flans came with a range of fillings. Sweet ones used almonds, cinnamon and sugar, while savory ones used cheese, curd, spinach or fish, which suited the meatless days of Lent in Spain.

Two other Italian cookbooks from the 14th century include recipes for Roman pastello and lasagna pie. They also call for the use of salt from Sardinia or Chioggia, showing that cooks named where their salt came from.

art.text: Around 1300, an influx of textiles from the Mongol Empire reached Italy and proved quite influential in Italian art. These textiles even revolutionized Italian textile designs.
art.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

art.text: Florence Cathedral was begun in 1296 to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio. The city took it so seriously as a civic monument that it financed it with a tax on all its male inhabitants. It even lowered the level of the streets around it so the building would be more visible.

Italian Gothic architecture differed considerably from its French origins. Italian builders kept traditional construction methods, cared less about soaring height, and often used brick rather than stone. Marble was widely used for decoration.

Around 1250, artistic developments in different Italian regions began to show shared characteristics. Before that, Italian art had been largely regional, shaped by local traditions and by influences from Western Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean. This led to a growing sense of unity and distinctively original styles.

Masaccio began the Early Renaissance in Italian painting in 1425. He is best known for the fresco cycle in the Brancacci Chapel, which he began with the older artist Masolino. It had a profound influence on later painters, including Michelangelo.

Around 1300, an influx of Mongol textiles reached Italy and proved influential in Italian art. Western merchants could buy such textiles from Tabriz and from Sultaniya, the Mongol capital established by Öljaitü between 1305 and 1313.
art.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

art.text: European artists imitated the Mongol 'Phags-pa script in their paintings, probably discovering it through Mongol paper money or paiza, the travel passes such as those issued to Marco Polo. In frescos at the Church of San Francesco in Assisi (1296–1300), saints study books written in pseudo-Mongol.
art.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

art.text: Cimabue and Giotto began to forge a more naturalistic and emotionally expressive approach to painting in the late 13th century, particularly in Florence. Even so, Italo-Byzantine painting continued in some regions and religious contexts well into the 15th century.

Giotto designed the campanile of Florence Cathedral, begun in 1334. After his death in 1337, work continued under Andrea Pisani and then, in the 1350s, Francesco Talenti. The square tower is decorated in marble panelling and follows the Italian Romanesque tradition, largely modelled after the older baptistery.
Ca' d'Oro, or "House of Gold", was built between 1421 and 1444 for Marco Contarini. Its portico and double gallery were originally gilded, which gave the palace its name.

Byzantine art strongly shaped Italian painting. Smaller Palaeologan artworks gained relic status in Western Europe, many of them looted in the 1204 Fourth Crusade, and they greatly influenced the Italo-Byzantine style of Cimabue, Duccio and later Giotto. Giotto is traditionally regarded by art historians as the inaugurator of Italian Renaissance painting.

In Giotto's The Crucifixion, painted between 1304 and 1313, soldiers wear tunics inscribed with pseudo-Mongol bands. In his Madonna and Child from 1320 to 1330, the Virgin Mary's robe has a hem in a mix of Arabic and Mongol script.
art.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

art.text: Around 1300, Mongol Empire textiles reached Italy and proved influential, even revolutionizing Italian textile designs. The Papal inventory of 1295 recorded large quantities of panni tartarici, or Tatar cloth, which must have been diplomatic gifts from the Il-Khanate.
art.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

art.text: Siena Cathedral has a most striking and original Gothic feature: a decorated screen facade on its west end. Giovanni Pisano designed its sculptural decoration and partly carved it between 1284 and 1320. The interior mixes Gothic and Romanesque elements, including horizontal banding of columns in polychrome marble.

Michelozzo Michelozzi designed the Palazzo Medici Riccardi for Cosimo de' Medici, commissioned in 1444. A decade later he built the Villa Medici, Fiesole. He also built the library at the Convent of San Marco in Florence.

Leon Battista Alberti applied the classical orders of columns to the three levels of the Palazzo Rucellai facade in Florence, between 1446 and 1451. At Santa Maria Novella he completed his design for the facade in 1456, but the work was not finished until 1470.
Byzantine artistic influence spread widely to Norman Sicily and to Venice. In Venice it can be seen in the mosaics of St Mark's Basilica.

Giotto and his pupils often combined Arabic and 'Phags-pa script in their paintings. In Giotto's Madonna and Child (1320–1330), the Virgin Mary's robe has a hem in a mix of Arabic and Mongol script. The Mongol script was probably discovered through paper money or travel passes such as those Marco Polo was issued.
art.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

art.text: The Silk Exchange in Valencia, built between 1482 and 1548, is an example of Gothic civil architecture in Spain. It was a major marketplace. Its main hall has twisting columns beneath a vaulted ceiling.

war.text: On 29 May 1176, near Legnano, Frederick Barbarossa's army of about 3,000 heavily equipped cavalry met a much larger communal army of approximately 12,000–15,000 men, most of them Milanese infantry from the Lombard League. The battle ended in a rout in which many imperial troops were killed, captured or drowned trying to cross the Ticino. The League had shown that autonomous communes could defeat an imperial field army commanded by the emperor himself.
Since the 13th century, armies in Italy had become primarily composed of mercenaries. This allowed prosperous city-states to field considerable forces despite their low populations.

In 1492, Granada was captured from the Moors, completing the Reconquista. This followed the 1469 marriage of Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon, which led to the creation of modern-day Spain.

At Legnano an initial imperial attack routed part of the League cavalry, and the imperial cavalry drove much of the mounted League force into retreat. The Milanese infantry nevertheless held a compact defensive position around the carroccio, in successive lines behind shields and long spears, which exposed attackers' horses as well as riders to injury. Imperial assaults continued for hours and failed to destroy this formation. Parts of the Lombard line were driven back, but a core remained in position.

In 1310 Henry VII of Germany crossed the Alps with 5,000 men, moved into Milan and had himself crowned king of Italy with a mock-up of the Iron Crown. He was crowned emperor in Rome in 1312. His plan to invade the Kingdom of Naples ended with his sudden death the next year.

During the 15th century the most powerful Italian city-states annexed their smaller neighbors. Florence took Pisa in 1406, and Venice captured Padua and Verona. The Duchy of Milan annexed nearby areas including Pavia and Parma.

The 1454 Treaty of Lodi ended the long-running Wars in Lombardy, which were driven by rivalry between Venice and Milan. The Italic League followed, and Lorenzo de' Medici was its main supporter. His death in April 1492 severely weakened the League.

In 1494 Ludovico Sforza, duke of Milan, sought the aid of Charles VIII of France against Venice, triggering the Italian War of 1494–98. Italy then became a battleground of the great European powers for the next sixty years.

Frederick Barbarossa captured Rome in 1167, which appeared to place Pope Alexander III in grave danger. Then disease devastated the imperial army and forced a rapid withdrawal. The sudden destruction of a large part of the imperial military establishment altered the balance in northern Italy.

Legnano did not end imperial authority in Italy, but negotiations resumed within months. The Peace of Venice of 1177 reconciled Frederick with Alexander III and set a six-year truce with the League. The Peace of Constance of 1183 then recognised extensive communal rights while preserving formal imperial supremacy.

Frederick Barbarossa's army besieged Alessandria from October 1174 until April 1175. Poor weather, flooding, shortages, desertion and the unexpected strength of its earthwork defences made the operation a costly failure. A final attempt to penetrate the city through a tunnel ended disastrously. With a major League relief army approaching, Frederick abandoned the siege and moved toward Pavia.

literature.text: In the early 13th century, Francis of Assisi was the first Italian poet, with his religious song Canticle of the Sun. Later, around 1300, Dante and Giotto were active in Florence, where capitalism and banking families were emerging.

Italian literature began in the 12th century, when the Italian vernacular started to be used in a literary manner in different regions of the peninsula. The Ritmo laurenziano is the first extant document of Italian literature. In 1230, the Sicilian School became notable for being the first style in standard Italian.

The Cantigas de Santa Maria are 420 poems with musical notation, written in Galician-Portuguese during the reign of Alfonso X The Wise. The manuscript was probably compiled from 1270 to 1280 and is highly decorated, with an illumination every 10 poems.

Romance literature was originally written in Old French, Old Occitan and Early Franco-Provençal, and later in Old Portuguese, Old Spanish, Middle English, Old Italian and Middle High German. The Old Italian romances are described as Sicilian poetry.

Italian prose of the 13th century was as abundant and varied as its poetry. Rustichello da Pisa composed many chivalrous romances derived from the Arthurian cycle. He then wrote the Travels of Marco Polo, which may have been dictated by Polo himself.

Giovanni Villani, born in 1300, was more of a chronicler than a historian. His Historie Fiorentine relates events up to 1347 and covers events all over Europe, thanks to his journeys in Italy and France. His brother Matteo continued it up to 1363, and Filippo Villani continued it again.

Brunetto Latini wrote his Tesoro in French, but also wrote works in Italian prose such as La rettorica, an adaptation from Cicero's De inventione. In 1267 Martino da Canale wrote a history of Venice in Old French.
The Florentine judge Bono Giamboni translated Orosius's Historiae adversus paganos and Vegetius's Epitoma rei militaris. He also wrote an allegorical novel called Libro de' Vizi e delle Virtudi.
tags: Libro de' Vizi e delle Virtudi

literature.text: The Alfonso X of the Cantigas is not certainly a composer. It remains unclear whether he composed the Cantigas de Santa Maria himself or was perhaps a compiler. He is known to have regularly invited musicians and poets to court, who were undoubtedly involved in their production.

Writers like Dante Alighieri, who died in 1321, and Marsilius of Padua expressed commitment to the principle of universal monarchy. They also backed the actual pretensions of Emperors Henry VII and Louis IV respectively.
Dino Compagni wrote a chronicle at the end of the 13th century that is probably authentic. Other chronicles once believed to date from the 13th century are now mainly regarded as forgeries.

Andrea of Grosseto, in 1268, translated three treatises of Albertanus of Brescia from Latin to Tuscan. Around the middle of the century, a writer named Aldobrando or Aldobrandino wrote a book for Beatrice of Savoy, called Le Régime du corps.

science.text: Iberia was part of the Islamic Golden Age of science, under rulers such as the Umayyads of Córdoba and the Abbadids of Seville. Islamic scientific achievements were especially strong in astronomy, mathematics and medicine. Scholars also studied alchemy, botany and geography.
science.source_title: Science in the medieval Islamic world

science.text: Between the 11th and 15th centuries, the first Western European universities were founded in places including Italy and Spain. They taught the arts and the higher disciplines of theology, law and medicine. Among the earliest were Bologna in 1088 and Salamanca in 1218.
Al-Zarqali (1028–1087) developed a more accurate astrolabe, and it was used for centuries afterwards. He also constructed a water clock in Toledo.
science.source_title: Science in the medieval Islamic world

science.text: In the early 13th century, schools of translation grew up in Italy and Sicily. Adelard of Bath travelled to Sicily and the Arab world, translating works on astronomy and mathematics, including the first complete translation of Euclid's Elements. Powerful Norman kings gathered men of knowledge into their courts as a sign of their prestige.

Al-Idrisi (1100–1166) drew a map of the world for Roger, the Norman King of Sicily, who ruled from 1105 to 1154. He also wrote the Tabula Rogeriana, or Book of Roger, a geographic study of the peoples, climates, resources and industries of the known world.
science.source_title: Science in the medieval Islamic world

science.text: Al-Zarqali discovered that the Sun's apogee moves slowly relative to the fixed stars. He also obtained a good estimate of its rate of change.
science.source_title: Science in the medieval Islamic world

science.text: Islamic science survived the initial Christian reconquest of Spain, including the fall of Seville in 1248, because work continued in eastern centres such as Persia. After the Spanish reconquest was completed in 1492, the Islamic world went into an economic and cultural decline.
science.source_title: Science in the medieval Islamic world

politics.text: By the 11th century, many Italian cities, including Venice, Milan, Florence, Genoa and Pisa, had grown into large trading centres. They were able to win independence from their formal sovereigns. Some of them later became duchies and maritime empires.

Italy's rate of urbanization reached 20%, making it the most urbanized society in the world at that time. The per capita income of northern Italy nearly tripled from the 11th century to the 15th century. Rapidly expanding commerce fueled this mobile, growing society.

By 1300, most Italian city republics had become princely states dominated by a signore, or lord. Venice, Florence, Genoa, Lucca and a few others remained republics in the face of an increasingly monarchic Europe.

In the 11th century the Normans occupied the Lombard and Byzantine possessions in Southern Italy. This ended a presence of both powers on the peninsula that had lasted six centuries. The Normans also ended Muslim rule in Sicily during the same century.

The Investiture Controversy between the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor gave Italian cities a chance to break from their feudal overlords. Milan led the Lombard cities against the emperors and defeated them, at the battles of Legnano in 1176 and Parma in 1248.

In 1158 the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I issued Authentica Habita, giving the first privileges to students in Bologna. In 1179 Pope Alexander III forbade masters of church schools from taking fees for granting the license to teach.

In 1310 King Henry VII of Germany crossed the Alps with 5,000 men, moved into Milan and had himself crowned king of Italy with a mock-up of the Iron Crown. Writers like Dante Alighieri expressed their commitment to the principle of universal monarchy and to the actual pretensions of Emperor Henry VII.

In 1395 Gian Galeazzo Visconti bought the title of Duke of Milan from King Wenceslaus for 100,000 gold florins. Such purchases let ruling lords win a noble title of sovereignty from their formal superior. By 1400 many of them had founded stable dynasties over their cities.

In 1155 Emperor Manuel I Komnenos made a last attempt to reassert Byzantine authority in Southern Italy, angered by Norman rule in former Byzantine territory. The attempt failed. In 1158 the Byzantines left Italy.

The Holy Roman Empire's effective control over Italy had largely disappeared by the High Middle Ages, though emperors never forgot their claims. Dante Alighieri, who died in 1321, and Marsilius of Padua expressed commitment to universal monarchy and backed Emperors Henry VII and Louis IV respectively.

According to Rashdall, universities in southern Italy and Spain lacked the independently evolving, self-regulating organization found elsewhere. They served the bureaucratic needs of monarchs and were, in his view, artificial creations of those rulers.

philosophy.text: The scholastic period of medieval philosophy is generally agreed to begin with Saint Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), an Italian philosopher, theologian and church official. He is famous as the originator of the ontological argument for the existence of God.

Scholasticism was less a philosophy than a method of learning. It stressed dialectical reasoning to extend knowledge by inference and to resolve contradictions, and it was the predominant education in Europe from about 1100 to 1700. Its schools flourished in Italy, France, Portugal, Spain and England.

Italian medieval philosophy was mainly Christian. It included St Thomas Aquinas, the foremost classical proponent of natural theology and the father of Thomism, who reintroduced Aristotelian philosophy to Christianity.

After a successful burst of Reconquista in the 12th century, Spain opened even further for Christian scholars. They encountered Judeo-Islamic philosophies and gained a wealth of Arab and Judaic knowledge of mathematics and astronomy.

The Dominican order was founded by St Dominic in 1215 to propagate and defend Christian doctrine. It used the new Aristotelian sources from the East and Moorish Spain. Its great thinkers were Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas, whose synthesis of Greek rationalism and Christian doctrine came to define Catholic philosophy.

Dante Alighieri (died 1321) and Marsilius of Padua (c. 1275 – c. 1342) both expressed a commitment to the principle of universal monarchy. Marsilius also backed the actual pretensions of Emperor Louis IV, and Dante those of Emperor Henry VII.
Adelard of Bath travelled to Spain and Sicily, translating works on astronomy and mathematics. His work included the first complete translation of Euclid's Elements into Latin.

In the middle half of the thirteenth century, William of Moerbeke translated and edited Greek philosophical texts. His work gave a clearer picture of Aristotle than the Arabic versions scholars had relied on, which had distorted the relation between Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy.

George Gemistus Plethon contributed to founding the Neoplatonic Academy in Florence. In the 15th century Pomponio Leto's Roman Academy symbolically restored the role of the Pontifex Maximus and celebrated the Natalis Romae. Pope Paul II dissolved that academy in 1468.

culture.text: By the 11th century, many Italian cities, including Venice, Milan, Florence, Genoa, Pisa, Lucca, Cremona, Siena and Perugia, had become large trading metropoles. They were able to win independence from their formal sovereigns. It is estimated that the per capita income of northern Italy nearly tripled from the 11th century to the 15th century.

Venice and Genoa were Europe's gateways to the East and producers of fine glass, while Florence was a centre of silk, wool, banking and jewellery. The wealth this generated enabled large public and private artistic projects to be commissioned.

The Black Death of 1348 struck Italy hard. Italy had been the economic capital of Western Europe and the top manufacturer of finished woolen products in the 14th century, but the plague, the birth of the English woolen industry and general warfare temporarily cost it that advantage.

The first universities were formed in Italian cities, and scholars such as Aquinas obtained international fame. Italy first felt the economic changes that led to the commercial revolution. Venice was able to sack the Byzantine capital and also finance Marco Polo's voyages to Asia.

In 1300 about 100 Mongols in Mongol dress visited Rome for the Papal Jubilee of Pope Boniface VIII. Such visits followed communications between Western and Il-Khanid rulers between 1265 and 1308, which led to numerous exchanges of people and presents.
culture.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

culture.text: By the late 15th century Italy was again in control of trade along the Mediterranean Sea. It found a new niche in luxury items like ceramics, glassware, lace and silk, as well as a temporary rebirth in the woolen industry.
